title: Design of biodegradable, room-temperature, hybrid non-isocyanate polyurethane foams from glycerol-derived cyclic carbonate
content: Polyurethane foams are widely used cellular polymers in construction, automotive, packaging and other applications, but their petrochemical origin, isocyanate-based production, and limited end-of-life options raise health and environmental concerns. Studies on non-isocyanate polyurethane foams have made important progress in recent years, but have not assessed the ability for materials to break down in typical composting environments. Here, we report a hybrid non-isocyanate polyurethane (HNIPU) foam platform based on diglycerol dicarbonate (DGDC), a linear cyclic carbonate derived from glycerol, and assess its total aerobic biodegradation in thermophilic temperatures using ASTM D5338. The HNIPU system leverages an exothermic epoxy-amine co-reaction strategy for ambient-condition foam fabrication, reducing reliance on external heating during processing. Systematic variation in epoxy loading triggers controlled in situ heat generation, giving formulation dependent maximum core temperatures (97.1–171.2 °C) and improved kinetic balance between gelation and blowing gas evolution to yield stable cellular structures with densities as low as ∼148 kg m−3. Bio-based modifiers, such as cellulose nanocrystals, cyclocarbonated lignin, and fatty-acid dimer diamine, were incorporated to further diversify the platform and demonstrate variable properties. Crucially, HNIPU foams were evaluated for end-of-life performance under industrial composting conditions, with selected samples achieving 60–62% carbon mineralization over 20 weeks. These findings provide proof of concept that key aspects of PU foam versatility can be translated into isocyanate-free chemistry with improved end-of-life benefits.
